title: Hamer v. Sidway
summary: Bargained-for surrender of a legal freedom supplied consideration even though abstention benefited the promisee and brought no financial benefit to the promisor.
notes:
Court: Court of Appeals of New York (1891).

The assignment structure explains why the named plaintiff was not the nephew. Do not confuse this case’s requested abstention with the unrequested retirement in Ricketts or with proof of mere reliance.

sections.Parties: Hamer, the holder of the nephew’s assigned claim, sued Sidway, the executor of the uncle’s estate. The underlying exchange was between William E. Story Sr. and his nephew William E. Story II.
sections.Material Facts: The uncle promised $5,000 if the nephew refrained from specified lawful activities, including drinking, smoking, swearing, and gambling, until age twenty-one. The nephew complied. On reaching twenty-one he wrote to the uncle, who acknowledged the entitlement and proposed to hold the money, with interest, until the nephew could manage it. The claim later passed by assignment.
sections.Procedural History: The Court of Appeals of New York reversed the intermediate court and restored the judgment supporting the claim. Some surrounding trust and limitations questions are omitted from the assigned opinion and are not independently reconstructed.
sections.Issue: Is requested abstention consideration where the promisee gains health or other advantages from it and the promisor receives no economic benefit?
sections.Holding: Yes. The nephew relinquished legal rights at the uncle’s request in exchange for the promise.
sections.Reasoning: The significance of detriment is the surrender of freedom to act, rather than whether the conduct made the nephew poorer or less healthy. Benefit to the promisor is unnecessary where a legally sufficient exchange is present. The notes refine this analysis through the bargain requirement: a merely accidental detriment, personal motive, or recitation of value does not establish that the act and promise were sought and given in exchange. The legal sufficiency of consideration is also distinct from the adequacy of its price.
